Q: nagios check_http HTTP CRITICAL - Unable to open TCP socket, works fine from command line A:

The answer to my question is: don't use check_http, use

  1. use check_https_hostname, and
  2. make sure that the host_name stanza is the actual hostname
  3. which requires matching the host_name stanzas in all the service and host definitions in the same cfg file.

So:

define service{
    use                     my-service         ; Name of service template to use
    host_name               www.example.com
    service_description     https://www.example.com
    check_command           check_https_hostname
    notifications_enabled   1
    retry_check_interval    2
    normal_check_interval   5
    contact_groups          myadmins
}

Here is why: it becomes clear by looking at the definitions of check_http and check_https_hostname which are in the /etc/nagios-plugins/config/http.cfg file in my installation.

# 'check_http' command definition
define command{
        command_name    check_http
        command_line    /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_http -H '$HOSTADDRESS$' -I '$HOSTADDRESS$' '$ARG1$'
        }

# 'check_https_hostname' command definition
define command{
        command_name    check_https_hostname
        command_line    /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_http --ssl -H '$HOSTNAME$' -I '$HOSTADDRESS$' '$ARG1$'
        }

You will notice that the -H and -I arguments in check_http get the same value $HOSTADDRESS$, while in check_https_hostname they get $HOSTNAME$ and $HOSTADDRESS$, respectively.

The fact that I built my original command as check_http!-I my.ip.address --ssl -H www.example.com did not really matter. In the end, the /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_http command got two values for -I and two for -H, and the second pair was being ignored.

This did break "thanks" to Cloudflare, because the IP address dynamically assigned by Cloudflare to my www.example.com was not the same as the actual host IP address that I had specified in my host definition.

Finally, I wanted to mention that what helped me figure this out was setting 

debug_level=-1
debug_verbosity=1

in my /etc/nagios3/nagios.cfg file and then looking through /var/log/nagios3/nagios.debug.

Also, check out all the different variants of the check_http commands in /etc/nagios-plugins/config/http.cfg. There are some very useful ones.

Q: AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'inverse_transform' A:

Suppose if we have done the encoding of y like

encoded_y = scaler.fit_transform(original_dataset)

then, the decoding of y (to bring it back to its original state) should be done like

y = scaler.inverse_transform(original_dataset)

This will ensure that y is decoded again with the same parameters with which it was encoded before.

Q: Delete old entries of the event-log with PowerShell? A:

I found a one-liner to remove ALL entries from ALL eventlogs e.g.

wevtutil el | Foreach-Object {Write-Host "Clearing $_"; wevtutil cl "$_"}

Personally I either set a limit on eventlog size

limit-eventLog -logname Security -MaximumSize 64KB

or do a monthly export and delete after export.

Q: How do two-phase commits prevent last-second failure? A:

The missing parts are

  • #3 is incorrect - the 2PC transaction is not corrupted
  • #4 is incorrect - nodes remain in the prepare state, including after crashing and restarting, until the coordinator requests rollback or commit
  • "I am assuming each node ... doesn't know anything about distributed transactions" is inconsistent "all nodes respond they are ready to commit" - either the nodes support 2PC or they do not

The reasoning: in two phase commit the coordinator can issue three idempotent commands to each of the nodes:

  • prepare: the node tries to tentatively accept the transaction with the ability to rollback on request. The node either enters the prepared state and responds with success, or fails and responds with failure and is not prepared.
    • a prepared node remains so until the coordinator requests rollback or commit. Even if it crashes and recovers. It does not know the state of other nodes involved so it cannot unilaterally rollback or commit without risking inconsistency. Hence why #3 and #4 are wrong.
    • entering the prepared state is also promises to the coordinator that the node will rollback or commit later without failing**
  • rollback: the node rolls back the tentative transaction, subsequent transactions proceed without its effects
  • commit: the node commits the tentative transaction, subsequent transactions proceed with its effects

2PC is both an API and related implementation features. It is not possible to do 2PC operations directly on a database that does not support 2PC - there is no prepare command for example. It is often possible put the database behind e.g. a custom REST API that implements 2PC using the database's features but that is beyond the scope of this answer.

** in reality failures can always occur, especially temporary ones like node crashes or network interruptions. But for the most part such temporary failures "only" lead to slow throughput and increased downtime, not consistency violations.

Q: How to scan the latest TRX block for transfer events to check if an address has a new transaction A:

To scan the latest TRX block for transactions on a specific address, you need to get the block details, and then loop through all transactions in that block to check if your address is involved.

Here is the working approach using tronpy:

from tronpy import Tron
client = Tron()
target_address = 'TTzPiwbBedv7E8p4FkyPyeqq4RVoqRL3TW'
latest_block = client.get_latest_block()
transactions = latest_block['transactions']
for tx in transactions:
    try:
        contract = tx['raw_data']['contract'][0]
        value = contract['parameter']['value']
        
        from_address = value.get('owner_address', '')
        to_address = value.get('to_address', '')
        amount = value.get('amount', 0)
        
        if target_address in [from_address, to_address]:
            print('New transaction found!')
            print('From:', from_address)
            print('To:', to_address)
            print('Amount:', amount / 1_000_000, 'TRX')
            print('TX ID:', tx['txID'])
    except:
        continue

If you want to keep scanning every new block continuously, wrap the above code in a while loop and use get_latest_block_number() to track which blocks you have already scanned so you do not scan the same block twice.

The key point is that each block contains a transactions list and each transaction has a raw_data field with contract details where you can find the sender and receiver addresses.
